claims.text: In HEAs outside the well-studied Nb–Ta and Ti-rich systems, superconductivity is governed primarily by average valence electron count.
Average valence electron count modulates the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level modulate electron–phonon coupling strength.
The proposed baseline is an equiatomic V–Cr–Mn–Fe–Co alloy, corresponding to 20 at.% of each element.
The baseline V–Cr–Mn–Fe–Co alloy has a uniform single-phase bcc or fcc structure.
Partial substitution of Cr by Mo will increase the average valence electron count.
Arc melting followed by homogenization will ensure phase purity and a single-phase structure throughout the alloy series.
The bcc or fcc lattice will remain structurally uniform while composition and electronic density are varied.
An optimal average electron-count range maximizes electron–phonon coupling.
Maximized electron–phonon coupling at the optimal electron count produces an enhanced superconducting transition temperature.
Electron counts away from the optimum reduce coupling efficiency and lower Tc.
Electron counts away from the optimum broaden the superconducting transition.
Tc will have a dome-like dependence on average electron count, with an intermediate composition having a higher Tc than the baseline.
Increasing or decreasing electron count beyond the optimum will suppress Tc and widen the superconducting transition.

The proposed mechanism applies only while the material remains a single-phase solid solution, every element remains at or above 5 at.%, and no structural transition or significant lattice distortion occurs.
BCS-based arguments establish a clear dome-like trend of Tc with electron count.
Lattice strain or local distortions could add effects to the proposed electron-count dependence.
Absence of a systematic dome-like correlation between adjusted electron count and Tc would falsify the primary electron-count hypothesis.
Large changes in Tc without corresponding changes in the density of states would falsify the proposed density-of-states mechanism.
